sources.title: Logan, Lively & Pisoni (1991): Training Japanese listeners to identify English /r/ and /l/: A first report
sources.locator: Methods B–C; Discussion; DOI 10.1121/1.1894649
sources.whatItSupports: Japanese adults; natural /r–l/ words, varied speakers and phonetic environments; held-out words and speaker tests.
sources.limitations: Identification training with visible alternatives, not this product’s cross-word audio-only ABX. Small initial study. Full stimulus table not recovered in this pass.
sources.license: Article copyright ASA; no recording-reuse permission inferred.

sources.title: Lively, Logan & Pisoni (1993): Training Japanese listeners to identify English /r/ and /l/. II
sources.locator: Experiments 1–2; DOI 10.1121/1.408177
sources.whatItSupports: Explicit investigation of talker and phonetic-environment variability for Japanese /r–l/ learning.
sources.limitations: Study-specific identification results do not establish an optimal number of voices or ABX superiority.

sources.title: Iverson, Hazan & Bannister (2005): Phonetic training with acoustic cue manipulations
sources.locator: JASA 118(5), 3267–3278; natural recordings and Appendix Table A1
sources.whatItSupports: Japanese adults trained on initial /r–l/ words; additional medial and cluster tests.
sources.limitations: British recordings; our American IPA is an editorial adaptation. Natural and manipulated identification conditions were compared; no blanket claim of superiority for manipulations.

sources.title: Iverson et al. (2005), Appendix Table A1: Words used in the experiment
sources.locator: Published paper p.3276, Table A1; full-text appendix inspected at this mirror
sources.whatItSupports: Exact lexical membership of the selected /r–l/ words marked stimulusSourceIds, including training, new-initial, medial and cluster sections.
sources.limitations: Membership only: not our American IPA, meanings, audio or training/test split. This inventory deliberately mixes original experimental roles and must create a new held-out split. Publisher DOI is the bibliographic authority.
sources.license: ASA copyright; no audio/images copied or reuse license inferred.

sources.title: Shinohara & Iverson (2018): High variability identification and discrimination training for Japanese speakers learning English /r–l/
sources.locator: Sections 2.2–2.4 and Discussion; DOI 10.1016/j.wocn.2017.11.002
sources.whatItSupports: Both identification and mixed discrimination training improved Japanese learners’ English /r–l/.
sources.limitations: The discrimination program mixed three tasks, including cross-word oddity. Speakers varied across sessions. Identification had a larger early identification-test gain. This was not our ABX algorithm.
sources.license: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 article; no commercial asset reuse inferred.

sources.title: Giannakopoulou, Brown, Clayards & Wonnacott (2017): High or low? Comparing high and low-variability phonetic training in adult and child second language learners
sources.locator: Stimuli and Training; Abstract; PeerJ 5:e3209
sources.whatItSupports: Greek children/adults trained on /i–ɪ/ with 20 real minimal pairs and tested with real and novel nonwords; five Southern British speakers recorded stimuli.
sources.limitations: Training used picture identification; no general high-variability advantage was established. Table S1 retrieval failed, so none of our words receives stimulus-list provenance from this paper.
sources.license: CC BY article; supplement/audio license not independently inspected.

sources.title: Nishi & Kewley-Port (2008): Non-native speech perception training using vowel subsets: Effects of vowels in sets and order of training
sources.locator: Abstract and study description; PubMed https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18664694/
sources.whatItSupports: Korean learners trained on nine American vowel categories; situates earlier Japanese nine-vowel training. Supports broader vowel-category coverage.
sources.limitations: Accessible indexed abstract/study description only in this pass; PMC body returned a browser challenge. Does not validate every binary contrast, word pool or task proposed here.

sources.title: Lambacher et al. (2001): Identification of English voiceless fricatives by Japanese listeners: The influence of vowel context on sensitivity and response bias
sources.locator: Methods 2.1–2.2; Table 1; Discussion, pp.334–343
sources.whatItSupports: 104 Japanese listeners identified /f,s,ʃ,θ,h/ in varied syllable/vowel contexts. Confusions motivate /θ–s/, /ʃ–s/ and /f–h/.
sources.limitations: Perception study, not an intervention trial. Stimuli were nonsense syllables; our real words are editorial. Vowel context materially changes difficulty, especially /ʃ–s/ near /i/ and /f–h/ near /u/.

sources.title: Leong et al. (2018): High variability phonetic training in adaptive adverse conditions is rapid, effective, and sustained
sources.locator: Experiment 1 Design and stimuli/Procedure; Experiments 2–3; DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0204888
sources.whatItSupports: Malaysian multilingual participants; /ɛ–æ/ training and tests including final /t–d/. Varied talkers and held-out items were considered.
sources.limitations: Training was same–different in babble; final /t–d/ was an untrained generalization contrast. Initial /t–d/ was near ceiling. No imported word list and no noise-training requirement inferred.
sources.license: CC BY article; no audio files copied.
